question: Why does Hobbes think that people are roughly equal by nature?
reference_answer: Differences of body and mind are not considerable when all is reckoned together: even the weakest has strength enough to kill the strongest, by secret machination or by confederacy with others.

question: What does Hobbes give as the three principal causes of quarrel in human nature?
reference_answer: Competition, diffidence (distrust) and glory.

question: According to Hobbes, what is the life of man like when there is no common power to keep everyone in awe?
reference_answer: A war of every man against every man, with no industry, arts, letters or society, and continual fear of violent death; the life of man is “solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short”.

question: What is Hobbes's first and fundamental law of nature?
reference_answer: “to seek peace, and follow it” (with the right of nature being to defend ourselves by all means we can).

question: How does Hobbes define injustice?
reference_answer: Injustice is “the not performance of covenant”; before a covenant is made, no action can be unjust.

question: Why does Hobbes think agreements between people are not enough to keep the peace without a sovereign?
reference_answer: Because our natural passions (partiality, pride, revenge) carry us against them: “covenants, without the sword, are but words, and of no strength to secure a man at all.”

question: According to Hobbes, when does a subject's obligation to obey the sovereign come to an end?
reference_answer: It lasts as long, and no longer, than the sovereign's power to protect them; the natural right to protect oneself cannot be given up by any covenant.

question: Where, for Hobbes, does the liberty of subjects lie?
reference_answer: In the silence of the law: where the sovereign has prescribed no rule, the subject is free to act or forbear at his own discretion.

question: Is Locke's state of nature a state where people can do whatever they like?
reference_answer: No. It is a state of liberty but not of licence: the law of nature (reason) teaches that, all being equal and independent, no one ought to harm another in his life, health, liberty or possessions.

question: How, according to Locke, does a person come to own something that was originally common to all?
reference_answer: Every man has a property in his own person and in the labour of his body; whatever he removes from the state of nature and mixes his labour with becomes his property.

question: Is there any limit to how much property a person may take from the common stock in Locke's account?
reference_answer: Yes: as much as anyone can make use of to any advantage of life before it spoils; whatever is beyond that is more than his share and belongs to others.

question: How does a person become a member of a political society, according to Locke?
reference_answer: Only by his own consent: by agreeing with other men to join and unite into a community for their comfortable, safe and peaceable living.

question: What does Locke say is the great and chief end of men uniting into commonwealths?
reference_answer: The preservation of their property (their lives, liberties and estates).

question: Can Locke's legislative power take a person's property without their consent?
reference_answer: No. The supreme power cannot take from any man any part of his property without his own consent, because preserving property is the end of government.

question: What is the 'one very simple principle' that Mill sets out in On Liberty?
reference_answer: The only purpose for which power can be rightfully exercised over any member of a civilised community, against his will, is to prevent harm to others; his own good is not sufficient warrant. Over himself, his own body and mind, the individual is sovereign.

question: Why does Mill think the 'tyranny of the majority' is not only a matter of laws passed by public authorities?
reference_answer: Because society itself can be the tyrant: through social opinion and feeling it can practise a tyranny more formidable than political oppression, penetrating into the details of life and enslaving the soul, so protection is needed against it too.

question: Does Mill's principle of liberty apply to everyone?
reference_answer: No. It applies only to human beings in the maturity of their faculties: not to children or young people below the legal age, nor to “barbarians” in backward states of society, for whom despotism is legitimate if the end is their improvement.

question: Why does Mill say mankind would not be justified in silencing one person who disagreed with everyone else?
reference_answer: If all mankind minus one were of one opinion, silencing that one would be no more justified than him silencing mankind: silencing an opinion robs the human race; if it is right, we lose the chance to exchange error for truth, and if wrong, the clearer perception of truth produced by its collision with error.

question: What happens to a true opinion that is never discussed, according to Mill?
reference_answer: However true it may be, if it is not fully, frequently and fearlessly discussed it will be held as a dead dogma, not a living truth.

question: What is Mill's position on state education?
reference_answer: The state should require (enforce) education for every child and help pay for those who cannot, but should not itself direct education; a general state education would mould people to be exactly like one another.

question: Hobbes and Locke both describe a 'state of nature'. How do their descriptions differ?
expected_source: Hobbes, Leviathan (1651);Locke, Second Treatise of Government (1689)
reference_answer: Hobbes: a war of every man against every man, where life is solitary, poor, nasty, brutish and short. Locke: a state of liberty but not of licence, governed by the law of nature (reason), which forbids harming others in life, health, liberty or possessions.

question: Why do people leave the state of nature and set up a government, according to Hobbes and to Locke?
expected_source: Hobbes, Leviathan (1651);Locke, Second Treatise of Government (1689)
reference_answer: Hobbes: for security, because covenants without the sword are but words and natural passions lead to war. Locke: to have a known and indifferent judge and settled law, because in the state of nature everyone is judge in his own case and men are partial to themselves.

question: Compare when Hobbes and Locke think subjects are released from obedience to their rulers.
expected_source: Hobbes, Leviathan (1651);Locke, Second Treatise of Government (1689)
reference_answer: Hobbes: only when the sovereign can no longer protect them. Locke: when rulers act contrary to their trust (e.g. seek absolute power over lives, liberties and estates); they forfeit their power and it devolves to the people, who may set up a new legislative.

question: Can a ruler wrong his subjects? Compare Hobbes's and Locke's answers.
expected_source: Hobbes, Leviathan (1651);Locke, Second Treatise of Government (1689)
reference_answer: Hobbes: no; since each subject is author of the sovereign's actions, whatever he does can be no injury to any subject. Locke: yes; government is dissolved when the legislative or prince acts contrary to their trust.

question: How do Hobbes and Mill differ on where individual liberty begins and ends under government?
reference_answer: Hobbes: liberty lies only in the silence of the law, wherever the sovereign has prescribed no rule. Mill: the individual is sovereign over himself; society may interfere only to prevent harm to others, whatever the law.

question: How do Locke and Mill see the power of the majority?
expected_source: Locke, Second Treatise of Government (1689);Mill, On Liberty (1859)
reference_answer: Locke: once a community is formed by everyone's consent, it must act by the will of the majority. Mill: the majority can itself be a tyrant, through law and through social opinion, so individuals need protection against it.

question: If Mill says the individual is sovereign over his own body, why does he accept that someone may be stopped from crossing an unsafe bridge?
reference_answer: The harm principle protects doing what one desires; a person who does not know a bridge is unsafe does not desire to fall in, so seizing him when there is no time to warn him is no real infringement of his liberty.

question: How is Locke's account of the origin of property connected to his limits on the legislative power?
reference_answer: Property comes from mixing one's labour with what is common, so it exists before government; since preserving property is the end of government, the legislative cannot take any part of it without the owner's consent.
